reason: Shore plants growing in the new soil seem a plausible way to clothe the wet ground.
expectation: This may establish vegetation on the wet ground.

reaction: The connection between underground support and plant height is clear.

reaction: The link between roots, light-gathering fronds and taller growth is clear.

expectation: This may establish fern growth on the wet ground.

effect: Moss and water automatically made a wetland, establishing another land habitat but not yet completing the forest goal.

effect: The wetland combined automatically with ferns to make the first forest, completing the remaining goal.
reaction: It was satisfying to see the apparently inactive ferns become useful, and the caveat about mosses not being unfinished trees was welcome.

mostWorthwhile.text: Making soil from shore plants and weathered rock was worthwhile: it made the transition onto land tangible while explaining that soil involves living and organic matter, not just wet rock.

leastWorthwhile.text: Trying water with ferns and then inspecting soil felt unproductive; neither revealed a route forward, although both narrowed the search.

surprise.text: Ferns initially had no available combinations, but later joined the wetland to create a forest. The spore-versus-seed distinction also clarified the spreading route.

arbitrary.text: Roots combining with light to produce ferns felt like a compressed symbolic leap, even though the explanation connected roots and light-gathering fronds to taller growth.

continue.text: I would continue: the progression from shore plants to soil, spores, wetland and forest made the developing world interesting, and the scientific qualifications helped distinguish the myth from a literal evolutionary sequence.
